title: No allocation on the hot path
objectives: Remove allocations from a hot path and write a pool allocator.

screens.title: Tap the allocations
screens.prose: A handler runs this function once for every market data message. An allocation asks the heap for memory. Assume a 100-character string is too long to live inside the `std::string` object itself.
screens.question: Tap every line that allocates.

hints.text: An allocation happens when a container grows or `new` runs.
A vector that has never held anything owns no memory yet.
Lines 3, 4, 5 and 6 allocate. Line 6 allocates a map node.

feedback.correct: Four allocations a message: lines 3, 4, 5 and 6.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for `new`, growth and long strings.

byKey.l2: You tapped an empty vector. It owns no memory until the first push.
byKey.l7: Arithmetic on locals lives in registers and on the stack.

explain.text: Line 3 gives the empty vector its first block and line 4 calls `new`. Line 5 needs a block for 100 characters, and line 6 allocates a map node. That is four allocations on every message.

screens.title: What one allocation costs
screens.prose: Assume a `malloc` or `new` costs 50 ns, and the feed sends 200,000 messages a second, one every 5 µs. Slide the allocations a message makes.

derive.caption: {{n}} a message: {{n * 10}} ms of every second.

screens.question: How many milliseconds a second does each allocation a message add?

hints.text: Cost per message first: one allocation is 50 ns.
Multiply by 200,000 messages and change nanoseconds to milliseconds.

feedback.correct: 10 ms for every allocation a message makes.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply 50 ns by the messages a second.

byKey.us: 10,000 is the figure in microseconds. The question asks for milliseconds.
byKey.ns: 50 ns is the cost of one call. Multiply by the 200,000 messages.

explain.text: One allocation is 50 ns, and there are 200,000 messages a second. That is 10,000,000 ns, or 10 ms, of every second. Each extra allocation adds the same again.

screens.title: Four allocations a message
screens.prose: The handler of the last screen makes four allocations a message. Each costs 50 ns, at 200,000 messages a second. Now and then an allocation asks the system for more memory, which takes microseconds.
screens.question: Fill in the cost.

hints.text: Four allocations at 50 ns each, per message.
200 ns a message, 40 ms a second, and 40 ms of 1,000 ms is 4%.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r2c1: 40 ms out of the 1,000 ms in a second.

explain.text: Four allocations cost 200 ns a message. At 200,000 messages that is 40 ms a second, 4% of a core. The rare slow allocation, which takes microseconds, hides inside that average.

screens.title: A pool of slots
screens.prose: A pool keeps its slots in a fixed array, and a free list runs through the free ones: each free slot holds the number of the next free slot. `allocate` takes the head, `release` puts a slot back at the head. Here two slots were allocated, then slot 0 was released.

state.caption: Pool of 4. Each free slot holds the next free slot. `used` is allocated.

screens.question: Tap the slot the next `allocate` returns.

hints.text: `allocate` always takes the head of the free list.
The head is the slot released last.
Slot 0 went back at the head, so slot 0 comes out first.

feedback.correct: Slot 0: the last released is the first reused.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which slot does the head point at?

byKey.c2: Slot 2 is next after slot 0, not first. The head is slot 0.
byKey.c1: Slot 1 is still in use. It is not on the free list.
byKey.c3: Slot 3 is last on the list, marked end.

explain.text: Releasing slot 0 made it the head and pointed it at slot 2. The next `allocate` pops the head, slot 0, and the head moves to slot 2. Both calls take a few instructions and touch no heap.

screens.title: What a pool saves
screens.prose: A pool allocation takes 2 ns, against 50 ns for `malloc`. Suppose the handler needs 3 allocations a message, at 200,000 messages a second.
screens.question: Fill in the cost of each.

hints.text: Three allocations, 200,000 messages: 600,000 calls a second.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the calls a second by each cost.

explain.text: There are 600,000 calls a second. At 50 ns that is 30 ms, and at 2 ns it is 1.2 ms. The pool is 25 times cheaper, and its cost never varies.

screens.title: Count the heap
screens.prose: A test can prove a hot path never allocates. Here the checker counts every `new`: `alloc_count()` reads the count, and the tests reset it first. The starter builds the text in a `std::vector`. Write `format_price` with no heap, using a small array on the stack.
screens.question: Finish `format_price` so the allocation count stays 0.

widget.how: Nine hidden tests: the text for eight prices, and one that formats twice and reads `alloc_count()`, which must be 0. The first Check downloads the C++ compiler, about 26 MB, and takes 10 to 15 s. Later Checks take a few seconds.

hints.text: Digits can be built into a `char` array on the stack.
Peel digits off with `% 10` and `/ 10`, then write them back in reverse.
Write the sign, then the pounds digits, a dot, and two pence digits. Pad pence below 10 with a zero.

feedback.correct: That's it. A stack array costs nothing from the heap.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

explain.text: A `char tmp[24]` lives on the stack, so building the digits there never calls `new`. The `alloc_count()` test would fail with the starter, which grows a vector. Pence below 10 need a leading zero, and a negative price needs a sign.

screens.title: Which one allocates
screens.prose: A colleague says every container allocates when it is declared, so declaring is the cost. We check four declarations and calls.
screens.question: Which of these allocates?

options.why: A default vector owns no memory yet. It allocates on the first push.
The eight ints are part of the object, on the stack here. No heap call.
A plain array of eight ints lives on the stack. No heap call.

hints.text: Which of the four has to ask for memory it does not have?
The empty vector has no buffer. The two arrays carry their own storage.
Only the first push needs a new block, so only it calls the allocator.

feedback.correct: The first push: the empty vector gets its block there.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which one has no memory until it is used?

byKey.decl: You blamed the declaration. An empty vector owns nothing yet.
byKey.array: `std::array` holds its elements inside itself, so it never allocates.
byKey.plain: A built-in array sits in the stack frame.

explain.text: A default vector has no buffer, so `push_back` must ask the heap for one. A `std::array` and a plain array hold their elements in place. To avoid the cost, call `reserve` before the first message.

screens.title: When the pool runs out
screens.prose: Every slot of a pool of 3 is in use, and a message needs a fourth. On the hot path the pool may not grow, and a slot released twice would corrupt the free list.

state.caption: A pool of 3, all in use. The free list is empty.

screens.question: What should `allocate` do?

options.text: Return -1 and let the caller decide

options.why: Growing allocates on the hot path, which is the cost we removed.

options.text: Wait until another slot is released
options.why: The one hot thread is the only one that releases, so it would wait for itself.

options.text: Hand out the oldest slot again
options.why: Two users would then share one slot and overwrite each other.

hints.text: Think about what the pool promised not to do.
It may not allocate, and a slot cannot belong to two users.
It must report that it is full and leave the choice to the caller.

feedback.correct: Return -1. Size the pool for the worst case, so it stays rare.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The pool may not allocate or share a slot.

byKey.grow: You grew the pool. That calls `new` on the hot path.
byKey.wait: With one thread there is no one to release a slot while it waits.
byKey.reuse: You handed one slot to two users, and they would corrupt each other.

explain.text: A full pool reports -1 and the caller decides: drop the message, or stop loudly. Size the pool for the worst case, so -1 never happens in practice. A slot released twice would link into the free list twice, so a debug build asserts on it.

screens.title: Allocate first, count after
screens.prose:
On a hot path every allocation is a cost and a risk. Allocate everything before the first message, from a pool or a fixed array, then prove it with a count. Free conference talk recordings on low-latency C++ for trading systems cover this ground.

```cpp
Pool pool(1500);          // all memory taken here
reset_alloc_count();
run_messages(pool);       // hot path
assert(alloc_count() == 0);
```
screens.question: Where must the memory for the hot path come from?

options.text: From a pool or array made up front
From a fast allocator called on each message
options.why: A fast `new` is still a call that can reach the system. The risk stays.

options.text: Always from the stack, never from a pool
options.why: The stack is one source. A pool covers objects that outlive a call.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. When is allocating safe?

byKey.fast: Even a quick `new` has a slow case.
byKey.stack: A pool is also fine: it takes its memory up front.

explain.text: Take the memory once, while nothing is waiting. After that every call pops or pushes a slot. The count test then proves the hot path never touches the heap.

screens.title: Write the pool
screens.prose: Now the pool itself. Slots are numbered from 0. `allocate` returns the most recently released slot, or -1 when none is free. The test at the end counts allocations over 100 rounds.
screens.question: Finish `Pool` so no call after the constructor touches the heap.

examples.setup: Pool p(3); int a = p.allocate(); int b = p.allocate(); p.allocate(); p.release(b);

tests.setup: Pool p(3); int a = p.allocate(); int b = p.allocate(); p.allocate(); p.release(b);
Pool p(3); int a = p.allocate(); int b = p.allocate(); p.release(a); p.release(b);
Pool p(3); int a = p.allocate(); int b = p.allocate(); p.release(a); p.release(b); p.allocate();
Pool p(2); p.allocate(); p.allocate(); p.release(0); p.allocate();
Pool p(2); p.allocate(); p.allocate(); p.release(0); p.release(1);
Pool p(8); reset_alloc_count(); for (int r = 0; r < 100; ++r) { int s = p.allocate(); p.release(s); }

widget.how: Ten hidden tests cover slot numbers, a full pool, release and reuse, and an empty pool. The last runs 100 allocate and release rounds, which must add 0 to `alloc_count()`.

hints.text: Keep one number per slot: the slot that follows it in the free list.
Build the list in the constructor: slot $s$ points at $s + 1$. `head_` starts at 0.
`allocate` returns `head_` and moves it to that slot's next. `release` points the slot at `head_`, then makes it the head.

feedback.correct: That's it. A free list threaded through the slots.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

explain.text: The constructor links every slot to the next. `allocate` pops the head and `release` pushes a slot back. The last released is reused first, and all of it is index arithmetic on reserved memory.

screens.title: Drill: the pool by hand
screens.prose: Drill: about two minutes each. Say the reasoning aloud first. Slots are numbered from 0 and the free list starts in order, 0 then 1 then 2.
screens.question: Fill in the slot each `allocate` returns.

rows: Pool of 3: allocate three, release 1, allocate
Pool of 3: allocate three, release 0, release 2, allocate
Pool of 3: allocate a fourth time with all three in use
Pool of 4: allocate four, release 3, 1, 2, then allocate twice: the second

hints.text: The head of the free list is the last slot released.
Release 0 then 2 makes 2 the head, with 0 after it.
Row 4: the heads come out 2, 1, 3, so the second allocation is 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r0c1: Only slot 1 was released, so it is the head.
byKey.r1c1: Slot 2 was released last, so it comes first.
byKey.r2c1: A full pool has no free slot to return.

explain.text: Each release pushes at the head, so the free list is a stack. Releasing 0 then 2 gives the order 2, 0. A full pool returns -1 and never grows.

screens.title: Follow-up: how big a pool
screens.prose: The interviewer asks: how big a pool for 1,000 live orders? Add a safety factor of 1.5 for bursts. An order is 24 bytes in the layout of level 1, or 32 bytes with padding. A core's L1 data cache holds 32 KiB, or 32,768 bytes.
screens.question: Fill in the pool size.

rows: Saving of the 24-byte slot over the 32-byte slot (%)

hints.text: Multiply the live orders by the safety factor.
Then multiply the slots by the bytes in one slot.
1,500 slots; 36,000 and 48,000 bytes; and $24 / 32$ is three quarters, so 25% less.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

explain.text: 1,500 slots at 24 bytes are 36,000 bytes, about 35 KiB, and at 32 bytes 48,000, about 47 KiB. Neither fits a 32 KiB L1, but the tighter layout is 25% smaller. A desk answer states the size and then says which part of it stays hot.

ideas: A message that allocates four times at 50 ns costs 40 ms of every second at 200,000 messages a second.
A pool keeps slots in a fixed array with a free list: allocate pops, release pushes, and a full pool returns -1.
Allocate before the first message, then count: `alloc_count()` stays 0 across the hot path.
summary.trap: Thinking an empty container allocates when it is declared.

quiz.prose: A handler makes 5 allocations a message. Each costs 50 ns, and the feed sends 150,000 messages a second.
quiz.question: How many milliseconds a second do the allocations take?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the cost of one message, then multiply.

byKey.us: 37,500 is microseconds. The question asks for milliseconds.

explain.text: 5 × 50 ns is 250 ns a message. At 150,000 messages that is 37,500,000 ns, or 37.5 ms, a second.

quiz.prose: Before the first message a program calls `v.reserve(1000)` on a `std::vector<int>`. Each message then pushes 500 values and clears the vector.
quiz.question: Does the hot path allocate?

options.text: No: the memory was taken in `reserve`, and `clear` keeps it

options.why: A push allocates only when the size passes the capacity.

options.text: Yes: `clear` frees the memory and the next push allocates again
options.why: `clear` destroys the elements but keeps the capacity.

options.text: Yes: once on the first message
options.why: `reserve` already did that work before the first message.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. When does a vector ask for more memory?

byKey.every: A push only allocates when the capacity is used up.
byKey.once: The reserve call paid for that already.

explain.text: `reserve(1000)` takes a block for 1,000 ints. Pushing 500 values stays inside it, and `clear` keeps the block for the next message.

quiz.prose: A pool of 5 slots. You allocate five times, then release slot 3, then slot 0, then allocate once.
quiz.question: Which slot does the last `allocate` return?

widget.accept: Slot 0: it was released last, so it is the head.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The last released slot is the next one allocated.

byKey.three: Slot 3 was released first. Slot 0 went back after it, so 0 is the head.

explain.text: Releasing 3 makes it the head. Releasing 0 then makes 0 the head, with 3 after it, so `allocate` returns 0.

quiz.prose: A pool must hold 800 live orders with a safety factor of 1.5. Each slot is 20 bytes.
quiz.question: How many bytes is the pool?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the slots first, then multiply by the slot size.

byKey.slots: 1,200 is the number of slots. Multiply by 20 bytes.
byKey.noSafety: 16,000 leaves out the safety factor of 1.5.

explain.text: 800 × 1.5 is 1,200 slots. At 20 bytes each that is 24,000 bytes.
